name: Elena Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and fit skirting, door trim and other finish carpentry on building sites. I have a trade certificate and years of steady work, though I am no master craftsperson. I like showing apprentices how to mark a clean corner, and I have never used an AI tool. My partner and I have grown children, a few months of expenses saved and retirement in sight; I would like to stop regular site work at sixty-seven in 2035 if our numbers allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices to learn the mitre saw before trusting a screen. An AI cut list cannot hide a rough corner in a newly built room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my usual wage and finish work to continue. A few months saved and some nearby builders give us time, but I still need regular pay until the retirement figures work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting trim and teaching the newer workers by example. I would ask my partner to check our planned age-sixty-seven retirement budget against what we actually spend, without claiming that enquiry is retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job itself. The budget question matters, but nothing in this picture seems to take my paid work away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show an apprentice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to scribe trim against an uneven wall, then check the joint from the doorway. A machine drawing is only a guide if the plaster wandered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the retirement budget look sound?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our expected income at sixty-seven would have to cover ordinary bills and repairs without running through our few months of cash. We have not decided to leave yet.

say: I would **keep** teaching apprentices to check trim against real walls.
I would **tell** the crew routine software does little to our hands-on work.
think: My **usual** wage looks secure, but age-sixty-seven retirement still needs a household budget.
A **few** months saved are a bridge, not proof that I can stop working.
do: **Keep** fitting building-site trim and showing apprentices clean corners.
**Review** our age-sixty-seven retirement budget with my partner against actual housing, food and repair costs.
feel: **Calm** about present work, attentive to later household income.
S0.quote: An AI cut list cannot hide a rough corner in a newly built room.
fieldNote: **Elena** favours familiar carpentry and apprenticeships, and has never used AI.
She **treats** a retirement budget review as information, not a decision to leave paid work.

steps.text: Keep fitting trim and teaching apprentices on site
Review age-sixty-seven retirement costs before any decision

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can order trim and book jobs faster, but the corners still need fitting by hand. If a new schedule leaves us waiting unpaid, I would tell the builder exactly which day it happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry management might shorten our paid finishing week after the planning work speeds up. We could manage a brief dip, yet several months of reduced wages would eat the money meant to carry us toward retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the trim shifts and record paid hours and delivery delays for the next few jobs. If hours are cut, I would ask for the rate in writing and apply to a posted nearby finishing job only if its wage covers our household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible wage dip in the years before I hope to retire. I can still check the books and use the local jobs that exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep a record instead of asking the builder immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record two or three jobs to show whether the paid delay keeps happening. A faster AI booking system could leave a finish carpenter waiting without pay beside a pile of missing trim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to avoid a cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used it and would not start just to look modern. I would first ask whether the builder has enough paid fitting work.

say: The **office** may plan faster, but I would record every unpaid trim delay.
I would **ask** for written wage terms if the paid finishing week shrinks.
think: A **few** months saved could disappear before my planned retirement.
I **prefer** measurable site evidence and a real local job to learning software for show.
do: **Record** paid trim hours and delivery delays on three building jobs.
**Keep** paid finish-carpentry shifts while asking for written rates.
**Apply** after cuts to posted local finishing job at household-covering wage.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic pre-retirement wage loss, with local options.
S1.quote: A faster AI booking system could leave a finish carpenter waiting without pay beside a pile of missing trim.
fieldNote: She **links** faster office work to a possible reduction in her own paid site week.
Her **resistance** to AI is stable; she would document hours and consider a real nearby role with adequate wages.

steps.text: Keep paid finishing shifts while documenting delay
Apply after cuts to posted local finishing job with adequate wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028 reaches me at sixty, but hands-on robots arrive around 2031 when I am sixty-three. A trim-fitting robot at sixty-three would reach my wage before I reach my planned retirement at sixty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my paid hours could shrink before I reach sixty-seven. A few months of savings would not replace four years of wages, and our grown children have their own households to manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid trim work and ask the builder for a written plan for human fitting hours through 2031. If robots cut my shifts, I would reduce optional spending and apply to posted nearby repair-carpentry jobs only at a wage that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the short runway, but I can still work and search. I would not retire at sixty-three without enough confirmed income for the years after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which job would you trust more than standard trim fitting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Repairing old doors and patching damaged trim, where each opening is different. I would need an actual posted local vacancy before leaving my current paid site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if shifts fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would put off a planned holiday and keep ordinary household repairs. I would not ask our grown children to carry the mortgage.

say: **Thinking** AI arrives in 2028, but trim-fitting robots around 2031 threaten my paid hours.
I would **not** leave before my age-sixty-seven target without enough retirement income.
think: **Four** possible wage years cannot be replaced by a few months of savings.
**Some** nearby repair work exists, but I need a posted opening and adequate pay.
do: **Ask** builder for written human trim hours through 2031.
**Delay** planned holiday if robots cut paid fitting shifts.
**Apply** after cuts to posted nearby repair role at household-covering wage.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible hours loss before planned retirement.
S2.quote: A trim-fitting robot at sixty-three would reach my wage before I reach my planned retirement at sixty-seven.
fieldNote: She **counts** the physical robot date, not the earlier thinking date, against her own retirement plan.
She would **not** treat the 2031 arrival as permission to retire without verified income.

steps.text: Keep paid trim work while seeking written future hours
Delay holiday after actual shift loss
Apply after cuts to posted local repair job with adequate pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2031 reaches me at sixty-three and hands-on robots around 2034 when I am sixty-six. That is only one year before the retirement age I hope for, so I would check the numbers before making promises at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot in 2034 could take the last paid year I was counting on before retirement. I might bridge it with savings, but only if our household income after sixty-seven and the remaining cash cover ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the finish-carpentry shifts and ask for a written retirement-cost calculation with my partner. If a posted local repair job offers a wage that covers bills for that final year, I would apply after any hours cut; I would not leave the site early merely because a robot is forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible final-year gap, yet I have time to count it. The calculation is an enquiry, not a notice to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would decide whether you can stop at sixty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our expected monthly retirement income must cover housing, food and repairs without draining the remaining savings. We will only decide after checking real figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an inspection course at sixty-six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it was funded, the training days were paid and a posted nearby role paid enough for our bills. I would not enroll just to fill one uncertain year.

say: The 2034 **robot** date is one year before my hoped-for retirement.
I would **keep** working while checking the actual income needed at sixty-seven.
think: A **lost** final year could hurt, and savings alone may not replace it.
A **course** enquiry is not enrollment; a local repair vacancy with adequate pay is more immediate.
do: **Keep** paid finish-carpentry shifts while checking retirement figures.
**Calculate** age-sixty-seven household income and bills with partner.
**Apply** after cuts to posted local repair job with household-covering wage.
feel: **Anxious** about possible final-year wage gap, with time to calculate.
S3.quote: A robot in 2034 could take the last paid year I was counting on before retirement.
fieldNote: Her **hoped-for** retirement at sixty-seven falls in 2035, one year after the 2034 physical robot date.
She **seeks** financial information while continuing paid work; any job application requires an actual adequate local vacancy.

steps.text: Keep paid trim shifts while calculating retirement
Check age-sixty-seven income against household bills
Apply after cuts to posted local repair role with adequate pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am sixty-eight, with capable hands-on robots around 2039 when I am seventy-one. If our numbers allow the planned retirement at sixty-seven in 2035, neither date catches me on a regular site shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A building robot in 2039 cannot take a wage I stopped needing in 2035, if our retirement sums hold. If we cannot stop at sixty-seven, I could be working when the thinking systems arrive and need a posted nearby fitting job at a decent wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep current trim shifts while my partner and I review our age-sixty-seven income and expenses. If the figures cover the household, I would retire at my existing target in 2035; if they do not, I would keep working and apply only to posted local finishing roles whose wage covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy until the figures are checked, but the robot date is less frightening in this picture. I do not need to claim a 2039 job I may never hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is retiring at sixty-seven an early exit because of robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It is the age I already had in mind, before this card. We would do it only if the household income and savings truly cover our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the budget does not work in 2035?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay in paid finish work and check actual nearby vacancies and wages. I would not lean on the grown children or assume a robot has already taken the job.

say: If **household** finances allow, I would retire at my existing age-sixty-seven target.
I would **keep** paid trim work if the budget requires it, using posted local openings.
think: The 2036 and 2039 **changes** may arrive after I leave regular site work.
I **cannot** claim retirement is affordable until our bills and income are checked.
do: **Keep** paid trim shifts while reviewing age-sixty-seven income and expenses.
**Retire** in 2035 only if verified household income covers ongoing bills.
**Apply** if work continues to posted local finishing job at household-covering wage.
feel: **Uneasy** until the retirement budget is verified, with distant robot risk.
S4.quote: A building robot in 2039 cannot take a wage I stopped needing in 2035, if our retirement sums hold.
fieldNote: Her **possible** 2035 retirement is her pre-existing target, not an early response to automation.
If the **budget** fails, she continues paid work and requires a posted local role at a household-covering wage.

steps.text: Keep paid trim work while verifying retirement budget
Retire at original 2035 target only if income covers household bills
Apply if still working to posted local finishing job at adequate wage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast case worries me most because robots could cut trim-fitting hours at sixty-three, four years before my planned retirement. Written hours and a real nearby repair job at enough pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens if the hoped-for age-sixty-seven budget fails. I will keep working, not pretend that grown children or a computer will pay the bills. My retirement date is written in pencil until the household bills agree with it.

headlineQuote: My retirement date is written in pencil until the household bills agree with it.
portrait: **Elena** is a fifty-eight-year-old trade-certified finish carpenter with a partner and grown children.
She **has** typical pay, one to six months saved and some nearby construction jobs.
She **has** never used AI, values apprenticeships and hopes to retire at sixty-seven in 2035 if affordable.
**Fast** robots threaten pre-retirement wages; the 2039 robots may arrive after her existing target if the budget works.
biggestWorry: **Robots** in the fast case could reduce paid trim work at sixty-three, four years before her hoped-for exit.
whatWouldHelp: **Written** paid-hour plans and a posted nearby repair job at a wage covering household bills would help.
